**OpenSearch monitoring metrics**

| Metric category | Metric | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Cluster health and key metrics | Cluster status | Shows the health of the entire cluster. Green: All primary and replica shards are allocated. The cluster is healthy. Yellow: All primary shards are allocated, but some replica shards are not. This indicates a risk of data loss. Red: Some primary shards are not allocated. Data is lost, and the cluster is unavailable. |
|   | Pending tasks | Shows the number of cluster-level tasks that have not yet been executed, such as creating indexes and allocating shards. A value that is consistently non-zero or increasing indicates that the master node is under excessive pressure or that there are issues in the cluster preventing task execution. |
|   | Shard status | Provides an overview of the overall shard situation in the cluster. Pay close attention to the number of unassigned shards. A value greater than 0 means that some data may be inaccessible or query performance may be degraded. |
|   | Memory usage | Shows the size of the physical memory (Resident Set Size) occupied by the JVM process on each node. This metric reflects the consumption of host memory resources by the node. |
|   | Disk usage | Monitors the disk usage percentage of the data path on each node. High disk usage (greater than 85%) triggers shard migration and can even cause the entire node to enter read-only mode, which severely affects cluster stability. |
|   | CPU usage | Shows the CPU usage percentage of each node. Consistently high CPU usage indicates that the node is under significant computational pressure, which may stem from complex queries, high-concurrency indexing operations, or background tasks. |

&M

|   | File descriptor usage | Shows the usage rate of file descriptors (FDs) on each node. FDs are valuable resources for handling files and network connections. A high usage rate (close to 100%) is a critical warning of a resource bottleneck. |
|---|---|---|
|   | Circuit breaker tripped count | Shows the total number of times the circuit breaker was tripped within the selected time range. The circuit breaker is designed to prevent the JVM from crashing due to an out- of-memory (OOM) error. Any value greater than 0 indicates that the node has experienced memory pressure and requires attention. |
|   | Number of nodes | Shows the total number of nodes and data nodes in the cluster. Data nodes are the core nodes that store data and perform operations such as indexing and searching. |
|   | Total documents | Shows the total number of documents contained in all indexes on each node in the cluster. This reflects the scale of data volume stored in the cluster. |
|   | HTTP connections | Shows the cumulative total number of connections established with each node through the HTTP protocol. This value's continuous growth reflects historical connection activity and does not directly represent the current number of instantaneous active connections. |
|   | Transport service connections | Shows the number of open connections for communication between nodes within the cluster (transport service). An abnormal increase in the number of connections may indicate communication problems between nodes or a risk of a split-brain scenario. |
|   | Open file descriptors | Shows the number of file handles currently open on each node. This is a key OS resource metric. An excessively high number (close to the system limit) will cause the node to be unable to open new files or accept new connections, leading to service interruption. |
|   | Circuit breaker usage | Shows the percentage of the parent circuit breaker's estimated memory relative to its limit. A ratio exceeding 80% requires attention, as it indicates that memory requests are approaching the threshold, which could lead to requests being rejected or even the circuit breaker being tripped. |

| sara Uni-manager Operati nsole |   |   |
|---|---|---|
| Resource usage and performance monitoring |   |   |
|   | GC frequency | Shows the frequency of JVM garbage collection (GC), grouped by node and GC type (Old/Young). Frequent GC, especially Old GC, introduces application pauses and severely affects query and indexing performance. |
|   | Cache hit ratio | Shows the hit ratio for the query cache and request cache. A high hit ratio (greater than 80%) means the cache is effective, which can significantly improve query performance and reduce CPU load. A low hit ratio indicates that the query patterns do not make good use of the cache or the cache is configured with a small size. |
|   | Indexing and query latency (key performance) | Shows the time taken for a single indexing operation and a single query operation. This is the most critical performance metric and directly affects user experience. A sudden increase in latency is usually related to resource bottlenecks (CPU, disk I/O), unreasonable queries, or data skew. |
| Thread pool monitoring | Key thread pool queue length | Shows the length of the task queue waiting for execution in key thread pools, such as the search and write thread pools. A persistent queue backlog is a direct signal of high node load. It indicates that the request rate exceeds the processing speed, which may lead to request timeouts or rejections. |
|   | Key thread pool active threads | Shows the number of active threads executing tasks in key thread pools. When the number of active threads consistently reaches the thread pool's maximum, it means the node's processing capacity has reached its limit, and new requests will wait in the queue. |
|   | Query time to fetch time ratio | This ratio helps identify the source of query bottlenecks. If it is much less than 1, it means time is mainly spent in the data fetching phase, possibly due to slow disk I/O or a low cache hit ratio. If it is close to or greater than 1, it means time is mainly spent in the query and computation phase, and the problem lies with the query itself or the CPU. |

&M

| Business error and anomaly detection |   |   |
|---|---|---|
|   | Cache eviction rate | Shows the rate at which fielddata and query caches evict existing data due to insufficient space. Frequent evictions indicate that the cache space is insufficient, preventing the cache from functioning effectively and increasing memory and CPU pressure. |
|   | Maximum task wait time | Shows the maximum time a cluster management task, such as shard allocation, waits in the queue. A large or continuously increasing value indicates that the master node is overloaded or that there are cluster- level issues blocking the execution of background tasks. |
|   | Write failure rate | Shows the rate (times/second) at which documents fail to be indexed for various reasons, such as mapping errors or a full disk. A value greater than 0 represents a risk of data loss and requires immediate investigation. |
|   | Scroll query rate | Shows the rate at which scroll queries are initiated. Scroll queries are suitable for paginating large amounts of data but consume node memory. High-concurrency or long- running scroll queries that are not closed are common performance killers. |
|   | Ingest current processing count | Shows the number of documents currently being processed in the Ingest pipeline. Ingest processing consumes CPU and memory. A consistently high value indicates significant pre-processing pressure. |
|   | Document indexing rate | Shows the number of documents successfully indexed per second. This metric reflects the cluster's write throughput and is key to evaluating its write capacity. |
|   | Indexing latency | Shows the average time taken for a single document indexing operation. Increased latency is usually related to resource bottlenecks (CPU, disk I/O), complex Ingest pipelines, or too many shards. |
|   | Search rate | Shows the number of queries executed per second. This metric reflects the cluster's query load and throughput. |

|   | Average query time | Shows the average time taken for a single query operation. This is the most critical metric for measuring query performance. High latency is usually caused by slow queries, data skew, or resource bottlenecks and directly affects user experience. |
|---|---|---|
|   | Document deletion rate | Shows the total number of documents marked for deletion in all indexes on each node in the cluster. A sudden increase in this value is usually related to many deletion operations. The space for these documents will be reclaimed during segment merging. |
| Indexing and search performance analysis |   |   |
|   | Current open search contexts | This metric directly reflects how many long- running queries, such as deep pagination or large aggregations, are currently active. If this value is high, it indicates that a potentially large number of slow queries are consuming node memory, which could lead to an OOM error. |
|   | Index throttle time percentage | Shows the percentage of total time that indexing operations spend waiting due to throttling. A high value indicates that the node's I/O or CPU resources are tight, and the system is actively limiting writes to protect stability, which reduces indexing throughput. |
|   | Merge throttle time percentage | Shows the percentage of total time that segment merge operations spend waiting due to throttling. A high value indicates that background merge operations are already putting significant pressure on I/O, and the system is actively limiting merges to prevent them from affecting foreground read and write performance. |
|   | Document merge rate | Shows the number of documents merged per second during the segment merge process. This metric reflects the intensity of background merge activities. A consistently high rate consumes a large amount of I/O and CPU resources. |
|   | Field data memory size | Shows the size of JVM heap memory occupied by field data used for sorting, aggregations, and other operations. This memory is uncontrollable and can easily spike due to improper queries, making it one of the main culprits of OOM errors. |

| Cache and memory monitoring |   |   |
|   | Query cache size | Shows the size of JVM heap memory occupied by the query cache. Monitoring its size helps evaluate cache configuration and prevents it from excessive expansion that could crowd out memory needed for other business operations. |
|   | Segment memory usage | Shows the total memory occupied by the segments of all indexes. Small, fragmented segments significantly increase memory overhead. Periodically performing a force merge can optimize segment memory usage. |
|   | Field data evictions | Shows the rate at which the fielddata cache evicts old data due to insufficient memory. Frequent evictions are a significant performance waste, meaning the fielddata cache is configured too small or there are serious issues with queries. |
|   | Query cache statistics | Provides a comprehensive view of the query cache's hit rate, miss rate, and eviction situation, used to evaluate the effectiveness and pressure on the query cache. |
|   | Segment count | Shows the total number of Lucene segments for all indexes on the node. An excessive number of segments consumes a large amount of memory and file handles and degrades query performance. Too many segments usually need to be optimized through a force merge. |
|   | Heap memory usage | Shows the usage percentage of JVM heap memory. This is the most important memory metric. A usage rate that is consistently above 85% will frequently trigger GC and may even lead to an OOM error. Healthy heap memory usage should show a sawtooth pattern, where usage increases and is then reclaimed by GC. |

&M &M

|   | Non-heap memory usage | Shows the usage of JVM non-heap memory, such as thread stacks, code caches, and class metadata. A continuous increase in non-heap memory is usually related to issues like class loading and thread creation. Although it does not happen often, it is difficult to troubleshoot when it does. |
|---|---|---|
| JVM monitoring |   |   |
|   | GC frequency | Shows the number of times JVM garbage collection (GC) occurs per second, grouped by node and GC type (Old/Young). Frequent GC, especially Old GC, introduces application pauses and severely affects query and indexing performance. |
|   | Average GC time | Shows the average time taken for a single GC operation. A long duration for a single GC can cause a lengthy 'Stop-The-World' pause in the application, and users will noticeably experience service stuttering. |
|   | JVM old generation memory usage | Specifically monitors the usage rate of the JVM old generation memory pool. The old generation space is used to store long-lived objects. A continuously rising usage rate indicates a memory leak or insufficient heap memory configuration and is the final warning before an OOM error. |
|   | Disk IO rate | Shows the rate of bytes read from and written to the disk for each node. High write I/O is usually related to indexing and merging, while high read I/O is related to queries. I/O capacity is the core performance bottleneck in disk- based scenarios. |
|   | Disk IO operations rate | Shows the rate of disk read and write operations for each node. This metric, combined with the byte rate, can help determine whether the I/O pattern is random or sequential read/write. |
|   | Inter-node network IO | Shows the network traffic for communication between nodes within the cluster. Queries and data replication, such as replica synchronization and shard migration, generate internal network traffic. |

&M

| Disk IO and network transfer monitoring |   |   |
|---|---|---|
|   | Inter-node packet rate | Shows the rate of network packets for communication between nodes within the cluster. For the same amount of traffic, a higher number of packets indicates greater network overhead and lower efficiency. |
|   | Transaction log size | Shows the total size of the transaction logs for all shards on each node. The translog ensures no data is lost, but an overly large translog will take a long time to recover. Its size is usually positively correlated with the indexing rate. |
|   | Uncommitted translog operations | Shows the number of operations that have not yet been flushed from the transaction log to the on-disk segment files. A continuously increasing value indicates high flush pressure and will increase the time for data restoration if the node goes down. |
|   | Current refresh listeners | Indicates how many queries are waiting for the index refresh to complete. If this value is consistently high, it means the indexing pressure is immense, new data cannot be made visible in time, and query requests may also be blocked, severely affecting real-time performance. |

Monitoring the number of currently active merges can help understand if the node is under significant pressure from background maintenance, which directly affects the latency of foreground requests. |

##### 8.2.4.3 View the Grafana monitoring dashboard for Elasticsearch

**for Elasticsearch**

This topic describes how to view the Grafana monitoring dashboard for Elasticsearch.

**Prerequisites**

You have obtained the endpoint, username, and password for the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console from the deployment team or an administrator. &M The endpoint format for the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console is `region-`

```
id.ops.console.intranet-domain-id.com .
```

Use the Chrome browser.
1. Open a browser.
2. In the address bar, enter the endpoint for the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console,
`region-id.aso.intranet-domain-id.com` , and press Enter.

> **Note:** You can click the current language in the upper-right corner to switch to another language. The console supports Simplified Chinese, English, and Traditional Chinese.

3. Enter your username and password.
&M

> **Note:** Obtain the username and password to log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console from the deployment team or an administrator.

If you enter an incorrect password three consecutive times, the image CAPTCHA feature is enabled. If you enter an incorrect password five consecutive times, your account is locked. Contact an administrator to unlock your account. When you log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console for the first time, you must change your password. Follow the prompts to complete the password change. For security, your password must meet the following requirements: Contain both uppercase and lowercase letters. Contain digits (0 to 9). Contain special characters, such as the exclamation point (!), at sign (@), pound sign (#), dollar sign ($), and percent sign (%). Be 10 to 20 characters in length.
4. Click **Log On**.
5. In the top menu bar, choose **Platform O&M > Apsara Infrastructure Management >**
**Kubernetes Management**.
6. On the **Cluster Overview** page, select the destination cluster. In the **Node List** section,
click **Node Performance Data** to the right of the target node to open the Grafana page.
7. Click the
icon in the upper-left corner to open **Tianjimon-Running Status-Details**.
8. In the navigation pane on the left, click the
icon. In the search box, enter Elasticsearch. In the search results, click the name of the Elasticsearch dashboard.
9. On the monitoring dashboard, select the target instance from the **Cluster** drop-down list at
the top to view the monitoring dashboard for the instance.

##### 8.2.4.4 Instance monitoring alerts

You can use the Grafana monitoring dashboard to view the monitoring metrics for your Elasticsearch cluster. This helps you understand the real-time status of the cluster, promptly address potential risks, and ensure stable operation. This topic describes the meaning of each monitoring metric, common causes of anomalies, and recommended actions.

**Monitoring metrics overview**

You can view the monitoring metrics of your Elasticsearch cluster in the Grafana monitoring dashboard. For more information, see View the Grafana monitoring dashboard for Elasticsearch. This topic covers the following metrics: Cluster_Health(Red) Cluster_Health(Yellow) Tripped for breakers CPU usage Avg JVM memory used Avg Active shards Relocating shards &M Unassigned shards GC time CPU and Memory-Load average Disk and Network-Disk IO throughput Disk and Network-Disk usage Thread Pool operations rejected Thread Pool operations queued Thread Pool thread active

**Cluster_Health(Red)**

**Metric meaning**

The cluster status is red when the primary shards of an index are not properly allocated.

**Root cause**

This anomaly indicates that some indexes in the cluster are unavailable and require immediate recovery. A common cause is a node failure, which prevents the reassignment of primary shards.

**Recommended actions**

log on to the Kibana console and run the following commands: Check the number of unassigned shards:

```
GET _cluster/health
```

Retrieve the reason why shards are unassigned:

```
GET _cat/shards?v&h=index,shard,prirep,state,unassigned.reason
```

Retrieve detailed reasons for unassigned shards, which explain why each node cannot allocate them:

```
GET _cluster/allocation/explain
```

If many shards are unassigned, you can check the reason for a specific shard:

```
GET _cluster/allocation/explain
```

`{`

```json
  "index": "indexName",
  "shard": shardNum,
  "primary": true
```

`}`

> **Note:** `indexName` is the index name, and `shardNum` is the shard number.

**Cluster_Health(Yellow)**

**Metric meaning**

The cluster status is yellow when the replica shards of an index are not properly allocated.

**Root cause**

&M This anomaly indicates that the cluster is operational but lacks replica allocation, which violates high availability (HA) principles. This increases the risk of data loss if a node fails. Common causes include insufficient hardware resources or multiple data nodes running on a single machine.

**Recommended actions**

log on to the Kibana console and run the following commands: Check whether node attributes, such as node_name and zone, are missing:

```
GET _cat/nodeattrs?v&s=node
```

Check whether the cluster settings include attribute configurations:

```
GET _cluster/settings? include_defaults&filter_path=*.cluster.routing.allocation.awareness
```

Check the number of unassigned shards:

```
GET _cluster/health
```

Retrieve the reason why shards are unassigned:

```
GET _cat/shards?v&h=index,shard,prirep,state,unassigned.reason
```

Retrieve detailed reasons for unassigned shards, which explain why each node cannot allocate them:

```
GET _cluster/allocation/explain
```

If many shards are unassigned, you can check the reason for a specific shard:

```
GET _cluster/allocation/explain
```

`{`

```json
  "index": "indexName",
  "shard": shardNum,
  "primary": false
```

`}`

> **Note:** `indexName` is the index name, and `shardNum` is the shard number.

**Tripped for breakers**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the number of circuit breakers triggered in the cluster. These include accounting, fielddata, in_flight_request, parent, and request.

**Abnormal effects**

A non-zero value indicates high memory pressure, which may cause errors such as Data too large or circuit_breaking_exception. It can also lead to partial data loss in responses from APIs such as _cat/nodes.

**Recommended actions**

1. In the Grafana dashboard, check the memory usage under CPU and Memory monitoring.
You can also review the Total disk operations rate metric to determine whether traffic has spiked.
2. Review your query statements for issues such as aggregations, wildcard characters, wide
&M time ranges, or queries that use the fielddata data structure.

> **Note:** Complex search queries on large indexes can cause the Tripped for breakers metric to spike.

3. log on to the Kibana console and run the following commands.
Check the node memory usage:

```
GET _cat/nodes?v&h=ram.percent
```

Check the memory used by inverted indexes (terms_memory_in_bytes):

```
GET _nodes/stats?filter_path=nodes.*.indices.segments,nodes.*.name&human
```

Clear the fielddata cache at the index level:

```
POST /index_name/_cache/clear?fielddata=true
```

Clear the fielddata cache at the cluster level:

```
POST */_cache/clear?fielddata=true
```

**CPU usage Avg**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the average CPU load across all nodes.

**Impact**

High CPU usage increases latency. If this metric exceeds 60%, the cluster is under pressure. If it remains above 80% for a long time, you should consider scaling out the cluster.

**JVM memory used Avg**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the average heap usage across all nodes in the cluster.

**Abnormal Impact**

Excessive heap usage degrades cluster performance. The recommended threshold is 80%. You should investigate if usage remains above this level for an extended period.

**Recommended actions**

1. In the Grafana dashboard, check whether heap usage remains high and review the GC
metrics.
2. If heap usage remains high, you can log on to the Kibana console and run the following
commands to analyze and resolve the issue.

**Segment memory inspection and cleanup**

Check the total segment memory on a single node:

```
GET _cat/nodes?v&h=name,sm
```

If segment memory is high, you can reduce it as follows: i. Delete unused indexes. ii. Close indexes and reopen them when needed.

**Fielddata memory inspection and cleanup**

&M Check the cluster-level fielddata:

```
GET _stats/fielddata?human
```

Check the fielddata on all nodes:

```
GET _nodes/stats/indices/fielddata?human
```

Check the fielddata for a specific index:

```
GET ${index_name}/_stats/fielddata?human
```

If the fielddata memory usage is high on any node, you can clear the cache as needed. Clear the cluster-level fielddata cache:

```
POST _cache/clear?fielddata=true
```

Clear the fielddata cache for a specific index:

```
POST ${index_name}/_cache/clear?fielddata=true
```

**Query cache inspection and cleanup**

Check the cluster-level query_cache:

```
GET _stats/query_cache?human
```

Check the query_cache on all nodes:

```
GET _nodes/stats/indices/query_cache?human
```

Check the query_cache on a specific node:

```
GET _nodes/${nodeName}/stats/indices/query_cache?human
```

Check the query_cache for a specific index:

```
GET ${my_index}/_stats/query_cache?human
```

If the query_cache memory usage is high on any node, you can clear the cache as needed. Clear the cluster-level query_cache:

```
POST _cache/clear?query=true
```

Clear the query_cache for a specific index:

```
POST ${index_name}/_cache/clear?query=true
```

**Active shards**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the total number of active shards in the cluster, including primary and replica shards. A single data node should have fewer than 900 shards.

**Impact**

Too many indexes can push the shard count close to the limit. You should promptly scale out the cluster or delete unused indexes.

**Recommended actions**

&M You can log on to the Kibana console and run GET _cat/allocation?v to retrieve the shard count for each node. If any node has more than 900 shards, you should scale out the cluster or delete unnecessary indexes.

**Relocating shards**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the number of shards that are currently being relocated.

**Abnormal impact**

Shard relocation consumes significant CPU and disk I/O resources.

**Unassigned shards**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the number of unassigned shards. Unassigned primary shards cause the cluster status to turn red. Unassigned replica shards cause it to turn yellow.

**Abnormal Impact**

Unassigned primary shards prevent normal cluster operation. Unassigned replica shards reduce high availability and negatively affect query performance.

**GC time**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the frequency of Java Virtual Machine (JVM) garbage collection (GC), measured in GC time per second.

**Impact**

Frequent GC consumes system resources and degrades cluster performance. The recommended threshold is 0.3 seconds. You should investigate if this metric remains above 0.3 seconds for an extended period.

**CPU and Memory-Load average**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the CPU pressure value. This value depends on the node specifications. For example, if a data node has 4 CPU cores, the maximum value is 4.

**Abnormal impact**

Excessive CPU pressure increases latency and can cause the cluster to become unresponsive.

**Disk and Network-Disk IO throughput**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the disk I/O speed. It shows the read and write rates for each node.

**Disk and Network-Disk usage**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the disk usage.

**Impact**

High disk usage negatively affects index creation and data writes. &M

**Thread Pool operations rejected**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the number of rejected messages in the cluster thread pool.

**Abnormal impacts**

A non-zero value indicates high cluster pressure, which causes some requests to be rejected.

**Thread Pool operations queued**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the number of messages in the thread pool message queue.

**Abnormal Impact**

Under high concurrency, Elasticsearch may queue client requests that cannot be processed immediately. If the queue becomes full, additional requests are rejected. A consistently nonzero value indicates high cluster pressure and requires attention.

**Thread Pool thread active**

**Metric meaning**

This metric represents the number of active threads in the cluster thread pool.

**Impacts of abnormalities**

The maximum thread count depends on the node specifications. For write and search threads, the limit typically matches the number of CPU cores. For example, a 4-core data node allows up to 4 write threads. If the write concurrency exceeds this limit, excess requests are queued, which is visible in the Thread Pool operations queued metric. If the queue becomes full, additional requests are rejected.

##### 8.2.4.5 Default monitoring alerts for the O&M platform

**platform**

The default monitoring alerts in the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console provide realtime insights into the operational status of your Elasticsearch service. These alerts help you identify and address potential threats promptly to ensure stable service operation. This topic describes each monitoring alert and its impact.

**View alert metrics**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console.
2. In the top menu bar, choose **Monitoring and Alerts > Alert Management > Alert List**.
3. On the **Alert List** page, search for **elasticsearch** in the **Resource Ownership** column to
view the default monitoring alert metrics for the Elasticsearch service. The Elasticsearch service supports the following alerts: Elasticsearch_health_up Elastic_Cluster_Health_RED Elastic_Cluster_Health_Yellow Elasticsearch_Pending_Tasks Elasticsearch_JVM_Heap_Too_High &M Elasticsearch_JVM_Heap_Warning Elasticsearch_Disk_Out_Of_Space Elasticsearch_Disk_Space_Low Elasticsearch_Cpu_Usage_Too_High Elasticsearch_Count_of_JVM_GC_Runs Elasticsearch_slow_young_gc Elasticsearch_slow_old_gc Elasticsearch_young_gc_surge Elasticsearch_old_gc_surge Elasticsearch_XDCR_Too_Many_Repository Elasticsearch_XDCR_Synchronize_Error Elasticsearch_XDCR_Synchronize_Max

> **Note:** In addition to the default monitoring and alerting metrics, you can also use the O&M platform to configure custom alerts based on your business scenarios. For more information, see **Apsara Stack O&M Platform User Guide** > **Alert Management** > **Alert Rules**.

**Elasticsearch_health_up**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered immediately when the cluster health status cannot be retrieved.

**Impact**

|   | cluster/health _ |
|---|---|
| cluster/health _ |   |

under excessive pressure or even unavailable.

**Elastic_Cluster_Health_RED**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered immediately if the cluster health status is red.

**Impact**

This indicates that at least one primary shard is unallocated.

**Elastic_Cluster_Health_Yellow**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the cluster health status is yellow for 5 minutes.

**Impact**

This indicates that one or more replica shards are unallocated, which affects the high availability (HA) of the cluster.

**Elasticsearch_Pending_Tasks**

&M

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if there are pending tasks in the cluster for 5 minutes.

**Elasticsearch_JVM_Heap_Too_High**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) heap usage exceeds 90% for 5 minutes.

**Impact**

The cluster is under high pressure, and the latency of some services may increase.

**Elasticsearch_JVM_Heap_Warning**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the JVM heap usage exceeds 80% for 5 minutes.

**Impact**

The cluster is under high pressure, and the latency of some services may increase.

**Elasticsearch_Disk_Out_Of_Space**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered immediately if the cluster's available disk space falls below 10%.

**Impact**

This may cause index write operations to fail.

**Elasticsearch_Disk_Space_Low**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the cluster's available disk space is less than 20% for 2 minutes.

**Impact**

Disk usage has reached the warning level.

**Elasticsearch_Cpu_Usage_Too_High**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the cluster CPU load reaches 90% or higher for 1 minute.

**Impact**

The cluster is under excessive pressure, and service latency increases.

**Elasticsearch_Count_of_JVM_GC_Runs**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the number of JVM garbage collection (GC) runs is greater than 5 per second for 1 minute.

**Elasticsearch_slow_young_gc**

&M

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered when the Young GC time exceeds 0.5 s per second for five consecutive minutes.

**Elasticsearch_slow_old_gc**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the Old GC time exceeds 0.8 s per second for 5 minutes.

**Elasticsearch_young_gc_surge**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the Young GC time exceeds 10 times the mean of the last 3 hours for 5 minutes.

**Elasticsearch_old_gc_surge**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the Old GC time exceeds 10 times the mean of the last 3 hours for 5 minutes.

**Elasticsearch_XDCR_Too_Many_Repository**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered in a cross-datacenter replication (XDCR) primary-secondary cluster setup if a secondary cluster is linked to multiple primary clusters.

**Impact**

XDCR synchronization is abnormal.

**Elasticsearch_XDCR_Synchronize_Error**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if write operations are occurring on the primary XDCR cluster, but the secondary cluster does not synchronize for 5 minutes.

**Impact**

Synchronization is abnormal, which affects disaster recovery.

**Elasticsearch_XDCR_Synchronize_Max**

**Alert description**

This alert is triggered if the index synchronization speed of the secondary cluster is slower than the index write speed of the primary cluster for 5 minutes. anagement

##### 9.1.1.1 Use the threat monitoring feature

Security administrators can use the threat monitoring feature to understand the overall security of a network. This topic describes how to use the threat monitoring feature.
1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console.
2. In the top navigation bar, click **Security Management** and choose **Security Operations**
**> Security Operations Center (SOC)**. On the **Security Operations Center** page, select
a region from the **Region** drop-down list and click **Access with Authorized Role**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Threat Monitoring**.
4. On the **Threat Monitoring** page, view the overall network security information within a
specific time range.

| Section | Description |
|---|---|
| Global Security Situation | This section displays the statistics on security risks from the perspective of global security management. The following list describes the modules in this section: Total Organizations: displays the number of organizations in the current cloud environment. Risk Index: displays the overall risk index that is measured based on the number of threat events and at-risk assets in the organization. Trend of Risk Indexes: displays the trend of the risk index. If you select Today or Last 24 Hours from the time picker, the trend is displayed by hour. If you select Last 7 Days or Last 30 Days from the time picker, the trend is displayed by day. Organization Risks: displays the statistics on the top 5 at-risk organizations, assets of the top 5 at-risk organizations, and threat events of the top 5 at-risk organizations. Asset Information: displays the total number of assets, the asset protection rate, and the proportions of high-risk, medium-risk, low-risk, and risk-free assets. Threat Events: displays the total number of threat events and the number of threat events at each risk level. The information about external risk sources and attack sources is displayed on maps. The world map and China map are supported. |

anagement

| Asset Risk Situation | The following list describes the statistics on the asset risk situation from the perspective of asset risk management: Asset Distribution by Risk Level: displays the distribution of assets at the following levels: high, medium, low, and risk-free. Trend of Asset Risks: displays the trend in the number of at-risk assets. The trends within the current day and last day are calculated by hour. The trends within the last seven days and last 30 days are calculated by day. Top 5 At-risk Assets: displays the top 5 at-risk assets, including the risk indicators, threat events, network attacks, suspicious behaviors, security vulnerabilities, and security baselines of the assets. |
|---|---|
| Threat Situation | The following list describes the statistics on the threat event situation from the perspective of threat event management: Threat Event Distribution by Level: displays the distribution and statistics on threat events at the following severity levels: emergency, serious, suspicious, moderate, and information. Trend of Threat Events: displays the trend in the number of threat events. If you select Today or Last 24 Hours from the time picker, the trend is displayed by hour. If you select Last 7 Days or Last 30 Days from the time picker, the trend is displayed by day. Threat Event Distribution by Type: displays the distribution and statistics on threat events in the following types: exception, malware, unauthorized privilege escalation, vulnerability exploitation, and risk connection. ATT&CK Attack Behavior: displays the statistics on ATT&CK involved in threat events. Top 10 Threat Events: displays the number of times that the top 10 threat events are detected. Threat Event Distribution by Attack Chain: displays the attack phases involved in threat events and the number of times that the threat events are detected. Attack phases include payload delivery, vulnerability exploitation, webshell insertion, command control, scan extension, privilege escalation, and target attack. |

###### 9.1.1.2.2 Use the threat investigation feature

The threat investigation feature allows you to perform comprehensive threat investigations based on IP addresses, asset names, and asset IDs. This topic describes how to use the threat investigation feature.

Suspicious Process: displays statistics on the suspicious processes in the asset in the form of charts and tables. Network Attack: displays statistics on the network attacks on the asset in the form of charts and tables. ###### 9.1.1.2.3 Use the cloud service check feature

You can use built-in security baselines to check and manage the security compliance of Apsara Stack services. This topic describes how to perform a cloud service check and view check data.
1. Log in to the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console.

to check and click **OK**.
5. Specify search conditions to search for baselines.
anagement

| Search condition | Description |
|---|---|

| Baseline name | The name of the baseline. You can enter a baseline name in the search box and click the icon to search for the baseline. |

7. Perform a cloud service check.
Manual check Click **Check Now**. The system starts a full check on the configurations of all services to detect risks and affected assets. During the check, you can click **View** to view the check progress in the **Check Item Detection** dialog box.

> **Note:** Do not perform other operations until the check is complete.

Automatic check Click **Check settings** to configure a check policy.

|---|---|

|---|---|
| Select Resource Set | The resource sets that you want to check. |
| Baseline Check Item | The baselines that you want to use. |

After you configure the check policy, Security Operations Center (SOC) automatically performs a check based on all specified baselines within the specified time range.
8. View the check results.

Find a baseline and click its name or click **Details** in the **Actions** column. In the panel that appears, view data on the Baseline Check Details and Cloud Service Instances tabs. If an organization or instance is riskless, you can select and add the organization or instance to the whitelist. Find a baseline and click **Verify** in the **Actions** column, or select multiple baselines and click **Verify** below the baseline list to verify that the detected baseline risks are fixed. During the verification for a baseline, click **View** in the Actions column of the baseline to view the verification progress. You can also click **Cancel Verification** in the Actions column of the baseline to cancel the verification.

###### 9.1.1.5.2 View platform logs

Platform logs record information about Apsara Stack Security. Security administrators can use these logs to troubleshoot issues that occur on Apsara Stack Security. This topic describes how to view platform logs.
1. Log in to the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console.
2. In the upper-right corner of the console, click **Safety management**, and select **Safe**
**operation > Security Operations Center**. On the **Security Operations Center**
authorization page, select a **Region** and click **Role-based access**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Logs > Platform Log**.
4. On the **Platform Log** page, specify the log source, time range, and query content based on
your business requirements. The following list describes the supported query syntax:

**Full-text match**

Example 1:

```
12.XX.XX.12
```

Example 2:

```
www.bai*.c?m
```

**Field-based query**

Example 1:

```
src_ip: 12.XX.XX.12 AND hostname:abc?o*al OR filesize:>100
```

Example 2:

```
12.XX.XX.12 AND appName:yundun-soc
```

The system displays logs in a column chart based on the specified filter conditions. You can view the numbers of logs at different points in time within a specific time range. You can also view the log details in the log list. To configure the fields that you want to display in the log list, click the icon. To export the log list, click the icon.
5. Optional. Click **Save as Analysis Rule**. In the **Create Rule** dialog box, the **Log Scope**
and **Search Condition** parameters are automatically configured based on the previous parameter settings. Configure the **Threat Name** parameter and click **OK**. For more information about parameter settings, see Create an analysis rule. After a rule is created, you can view the rule whose type is **Custom Association Rule** on the **Analytic Rules** page.

Find the log source and click **View Unrecognized Logs** in the **Actions** column. b. In the **Edit** panel, process unidentified logs. If **No Matched Parsing Rules** is displayed in the Why Not Recognized column, click
**Create Log Parsing Template** and configure the parameters.
a. In the **Rule Information** step, configure the **Rule Name** and **Log Type** parameters and click **Next**. b. In the **Log Parsing** step, configure the **Log Sample**, **Log Identifier**, and **Parsing**
**Method** parameters, and click **Next**. Then, complete the **Log Standardization**
step. If a different value is displayed in the Why Not Recognized column, click **Edit Log**
**Parsing Rule** to modify the existing rules based on the value, or click **Create Rule**
to create a parsing rule for the log source. You can **modify** or **delete** a log source based on your business requirements.

###### 9.1.1.5.4.2 Configure a log parsing template

Security Operations Center (SOC) provides the log parsing feature. Security administrators can configure log parsing templates based on their business requirements to manage logs in an efficient manner. This topic describes how to configure a log parsing template.
1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console.
2. In the top navigation bar, choose **Security** > **Global Platform Security > Security**
**Operations Center**. On the **Security Operations Center** page, select a region from the
**Region** drop-down list and click **Access with Authorized Role**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Logs > Log Configurations**.
4. On the **Log Parsing** tab, click **Create Log Parsing Template**.
5. In the **Create Log Parsing Template** wizard, configure the **Template Name** and **Scope**
parameters. Then, click **Next**. The values of the **Template Name** and **Scope** parameters can be up to 200 characters in length.
6. Click **Create Rule** to create a rule that is associated with the log parsing template.
Configure the rule information. Configure the **Rule Name** and **Log Type** parameters. Then, click **Next**. anagement The value of the **Rule Name** parameter can be up to 15 characters in length. Valid values of the Log Type parameter: **System Log**, **Operation Log**, **Network Log**,
**Threat Log**, **Application Log**, and **Other**.
Specify a log parsing method. Configure the **Log Sample**, **Log Identifier**, and **Parsing Method** parameters. Then, click **Parse**. After the parsing is complete, click **Next**. Click **Add** to specify multiple parsing methods. Valid values of the Parsing Method parameter: json jsonCut jsonArray jsonArrayCut grok keyvalue Specify field mappings to format logs. Specify field mappings to format logs and click **Confirm**. If you want to create multiple rules, repeat the preceding steps.
7. After all rules are created, click **Confirmation**.
The log parsing template that you created is displayed in the log parsing list. You can modify or delete the template based on your business requirements.

##### 9.1.1.6 Policy management

###### 9.1.1.6.1 Create an analysis rule

You can perform comprehensive association analysis on a large number of logs based on the analysis logic of an analysis rule to detect threats and risks and trace attack paths of multiphase attacks. This way, security administrators can obtain helpful risk information in an efficient and quick manner and the efficiency of security operations is improved. This topic describes how to create a custom analysis rule. This topic describes how to create an analysis rule. anagement

**Create a rule**

Security Operations Center (SOC) provides built-in rules based on common business requirements. You can only view the details of the built-in rules but cannot modify the rules. If the built-in rules cannot meet your business requirements, you can perform the following operations to create a rule:
1. Log in to the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console.
2. In the upper-right corner of the console, click **Safety management**, and select **Safe**
**operation > Security Operations Center**. On the **Security Operations Center**
authorization page, select a **Region** and click **Role-based access**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Policies > Analytic Rules**.
4. On the **Analytic Rules** page, click **Create Rule**. On the page that appears, configure the
parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Threat Name | Specify a name for a threat. |
| Threat Level | Select a level for the threat. Valid values: Information Suspicious Moderate Serious Urgent |
| Threat Type | Select one or more types for the threat. Valid values: Network Scanning Vulnerability Exploitation Malware Network Attack Suspicious Network Connection Suspicious Process Unauthorized Privilege Escalation |
| ATT&CK ID | Enter the IDs of one or more attacks that are involved in the Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK) stages. |

anagement

| Rule Type | Specify the type for the rule that you want to create. If you select Association-based Analysis Rule, you must configure the following parameters: Time Series: the time condition for the rule that you want to create. Valid values: Periodicity: indicates that the rule is used to detect the threats that occur within the same period of time. Chronological Order: indicates that the rule is used to detect the threats that occur in sequence. Sequential Occurrence in Same Cycle: indicates that the rule is used to detect the threats that occur in sequence within the same period of time. Associated Object: the object on which the rule is used to detect threats. The value is fixed as Same Asset. By default, this value is selected. Trigger Condition: the trigger condition. You can configure the following parameters to specify the trigger condition: Note On the right side, you can click Add, Delete, Up, and Down. Association Type: specifies whether the associated condition is a required condition. Log Scope: the log source, log type, log subtype, and log level. You can select multiple log types. Source IP and Destination IP. Keyword: If you specify multiple keywords, separate them with semicolons (;). Click Add on the right side to add a keyword. Match Threat Intelligence: specifies whether to match threat intelligence. If you select Match Threat Intelligence, select one or multiple keywords from the Reference Keyword drop-down list. You can select Source IP Address, Destination IP Address, Domain Name, and File MD5 Hash Value. Time Period: Unit: Minutes, Hours, or Days (a maximum of 365 days). Log Quantity: the number of logs. Attack Phase. Valid values: Payload Delivery, Vulnerability Exploitation, Backdoor Installation, Command and Control, Scanning, Permission elevation and Action on Objectives. If you select Search-based Analysis Rule, you must configure the following parameters: Data Scope: Select Platform. Search Condition: Specify search conditions for the rule. Time Period: the time period of a rule. |
|---|---|

anagement

| Execution Period | Specify the interval at which the rule is executed. Default value: 5. Unit: minutes. The following units are supported: Minutes, Hours, or Days (a maximum of 365 days). |
|---|---|
| Description | Enter the description of the threat. The description can be 0 to 256 characters in length. |
| Handling Suggestion | Enter the handling suggestion. The suggestion can be 0 to 256 characters in length. |

5. **(Optional)** If you want to verify the rule that you create, click **Quick Verify**.
6. Click **OK**.
The created rule is displayed in the rule list. You can click **Edit** or **Delete** in the Actions column of a custom rule to modify or delete the rule based on your business requirements.

**Manage a rule**

1. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Policies > Analytic Rules**.
2. In the rule list, you can view the following information about a rule: the rule ID, threat
name, threat level, threat type, organization, data range, ATT&CK ID, rule type, and status. You can also perform the following operations to manage a rule:

**Change the rule status**

In the **Status** column, click the switch icon to enable or disable the rule.

**Edit or delete the rule**

In the rule list, click **Edit** or **Delete** in the **Actions** column.

**Copy a rule**

In the rule list, click **Copy** in the **Actions** column. In the **Copy Rule** dialog box, select an organization from the **Organization** drop-down list and click **OK**. This operation is applicable to specific rules. If one or more predefined rules are disabled, **the system prompts you to**

**confirm whether to enable them.**

> You can edit or delete a custom rule that is created based on the Copy operation. You can delete a predefined rule that is created based on the Copy operation.

###### 9.1.1.6.2 Create a response policy

You can create a response policy to quickly handle threat events and security alerts (security alerts on the Operations Center page), and monitor risk information related to threat events, security alerts (security alerts on the Operations Center page), security baselines, and security vulnerabilities. Real-time alert notifications are sent to specified contacts via DingTalk or email. This topic describes how to create a response policy. anagement

**Create a response policy**

To create a response policy, perform the following operations:
1. Log in to the Apsara Uni-manager Operations Console.
2. In the upper-right corner of the console, click **Safety management**, and select **Safe**
**operation > Security Operations Center**. On the **Security Operations Center**

### 9.2 Network security

anagement

#### 9.2.1 Web Application Firewall (WAF)

##### 9.2.1.1 Protection configuration

###### 9.2.1.1.1 Add a website to WAF for protection

Compared with tenant-side Web Application Firewall (WAF), platform-side WAF is used to manage the status of intrusion protection configurations at the WAF platform management side and the service group management side. Platform-side WAF performs intrusion detection and request processing on platform-side web traffic. If you want WAF to perform actions on traffic to a specific domain name, you must add the domain name to WAF. This topic describes how to add a domain name to WAF.

**Background information**

The following list describes the default configurations of platform-side WAF: By default, **HTTPS proxy traffic forwarding** and **ingress traffic forwarding** are disabled. If the wildcard character (*) is used as a part of the domain name of a protected website and **Platform Observation Mode** is configured for the website, WAF records requests to the website but does not block the requests. The configurations of the website cannot be modified. If you want to block requests to a specific domain name, you must enable **HTTPS proxy traffic forwarding**, add the HTTPS proxy to WAF, and configure protection policies.

**Prerequisites**

Your account is assigned the **platform security configuration administrator** role. For more information, see User roles and permissions.
1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console.
2. In the upper-right corner of the console, choose
> **User Information**.

3. On the page that appears, click **Switch Role**. In the Switch Role dialog box, select
**Platform Security Configuration Administrator** from the **Switch Role** drop-down list.
4. In the upper-right corner of the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console, choose
**Security** > **Application Security > Web Application Firewall**. On the **Web**
**Application Firewall** page, select a **region** and click **Access with Authorized Role**.
5. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **System Settings** > **Global System Settings** and
enable **https-proxy traffic forwarding**.
6. Obtain the domain name.
i. Log on to Apsara Infrastructure Management. ii. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **O&M Tools** > **Basic Data Management**. anagement iii. On the **Basic Data Management** page, click **Resource Dashboard**. Enter
**https_proxy** in the **Name** search box to obtain the logon information and the values of
`db_host` , `db_user` , `db_password` , `db_password` , and `db_name` . iv. Run the following command on the OPS server and log on to the database:

```
mysql -h{db_host} -u{db_user} -p{db_password} -P{db_port} -D{db_name}
```

v. Run the following command to obtain the domain name of the HTTPS proxy:

```
select * from domain_info\G;
```

7. Add the obtained domain name to WAF.
i. In the upper-right corner of the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console, choose
**Security** > **Application Security > Web Application Firewall**. On the **Web**
**Application Firewall** page, select a **region** and click **Access with Authorized Role**.
ii. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Protection Configuration** > **Protection Site**
**Management**.
iii. On the **Internet Websites** tab, click **Add a site**. iv. In the **Monitoring Information** step of the **Add Protected Site** panel, configure the parameters and click **Next**. The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Protected Website Name | The name of the website that you want WAF to protect. |
| Domain Name | The domain name of the website. You cannot use an asterisk (*) as a wildcard. If you specify multiple domain names, separate them with commas (,). |
| Description | The description of the website. |
| Port settings | The port on which WAF listens. If the website can be accessed over multiple ports, click Add a group of ports to add the ports. |

anagement v. In the **Protection Policy** step of the **Add Protected Site** panel, configure the parameters and click **Next**. Then, go to the **Finish** step. The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Protection Policy | Select a WAF protection policy. By default, Default Policy Set is selected. Valid values: Disable Protection Policy Default protection policies Default Policy Set Strict Protection Internet Enterprise Internet Enterprise Observation Mode Platform Observation Mode Custom protection policy For information about the preceding protection policies, see Configure protection policies. |
| User Identification | Specify whether to enable the user identification feature. Valid values: Disable, WAF User System, and Extract User ID from Request. Note If you enabled HTTP flood protection for the protected website and set the Target Type parameter to SESSION when you configured the HTTP flood protection rule, you must set the User Identification parameter to WAF User System. If you set the User Identification parameter to Extract User ID from Request, you must configure the User ID Locates in and User ID Parameter parameters. |

After you add a website to WAF, WAF processes attacks that match the protection rule. You can perform the following operations on the protected website list. View protected websites anagement You can view information about the Internet websites that you added to WAF, such as the status, name, port, domain name, and protection policy. Specify the items that you want to view in the protected website list. Click the icon to the right of **Actions** and select the items that you want to view in the protected website list. Filter Internet websites In the upper-right corner of the Protection Site Management page, click **Filter** and specify filter conditions, such as the name, domain name, protection policy, status of the website tamper-proofing feature, creation time, and most recent modification time. Enable, disable, export, or delete protected websites Select the protected websites that you want to manage. Select **Enable Selected Sites**,
**Disable Selected Sites**, **Export Selected Sites**, or **Delete Selected Sites** from the
**More** drop-down list.
Modify basic information about protected websites Find the protected website whose basic information you want to modify and click the icon in the **Actions** column. On the **Basic Information** tab, click the icon to the right of each configuration item to modify the corresponding information. You can modify the following information about the website on the Basic Information tab: name, listening port, domain name, and remarks. Modify the method of recording logs Click the icon in the **Actions** column. On the **Request Processing Method** tab, click the icon to the right of **Access Log Record** to modify the method of recording logs. View and modify protection methods Website Protection Policies: View the details of the protection policies that you configured, such as decoding methods, attack detection modules, block options, HTTP response processing, HTTP request body detection, and detection timeout. Click the icon to the right of Default Policy Set to modify protection policies. For more information about protection policies, see Configure protection policies. Customize Rules: You can click Add Customized Rule to add custom rules in the Customize Rules section. For more information, see Create a custom rule. anagement Source IP Recording Options: You can specify the method to obtain the IP address of the origin server. The IP address of the origin server can be obtained from the X- Forwarded-For header. User Identification: You can specify the method to identify users. For more information, see the description of the User Identification parameter in this topic.

###### 9.2.1.1.2 Configure protection policies

Web Application Firewall (WAF) provides default protection policies. You can also configure custom protection policies. This topic describes how to configure custom protection policies.

**Background information**

The following table describes the default protection policies that are provided by WAF.

| Protection policy | Scenario | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Default protection policy | Scenarios that do not have high security requirements | Blocks high-risk attacks but does not detect server responses and bot requests. |
| Strict protection policy | Scenarios that have high security requirements | Blocks all attacks. |
| Policy for Internet enterprises | Website services | Blocks high-risk attacks but does not detect Active Server Pages (ASP) code injection attacks and module injection attacks. |
| Policy for financial institutions | Financial website services | Allows and records command injection attacks, blocks high-risk attacks, but does not detect ASP code injection attacks and module injection attacks. |
| Policy in monitoring mode | Scenarios in which attacks need to only be recorded | Allows and records all requests. |
| Policy in platform monitoring mode | Scenarios that do not have high security requirements | Allows and records all requests. Note This protection policy is displayed only if the user role is platform security configuration administrator. |

To configure custom protection policies, perform the following steps: 1. anagement
2. In the top navigation bar, choose **Security Management > Network Security > Web**
**Application Firewall**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Protection Configuration > Website**
**Protection Policies**.
4. In the upper-right corner of the Website Protection Policies page, click **Add a protection**
**policy**. In the panel that appears, configure the **Policy name** parameter and click
**Confirm**.
5. Find the new protection policy and click the
icon in the **Actions** column. On the Protection Policy Details page, configure the parameters. The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Decode | The algorithms that you want to use to decode the requests. |
| Attack Detection Modules | The types of attacks that you want to detect and the risk levels of attacks that you want to block. |
| Other Modules | You do not need to configure this parameter. |
| Block Options | The HTTP status code and image that you want WAF to return when WAF blocks an attack. |
| HTTP Response Processing | The status of HTTP response processing. You can set this parameter to ON or OFF to enable or disable HTTP response processing. |
| HTTP Request Body Detection | The threshold for HTTP request body detection. |
| Detection Timeout | Configure the Enable Detection Timeout and Timeout Threshold parameters. |

For example, perform the following steps to configure detection modules in the **Attack**
**Detection Modules** section:
i. Find a specific module in the **Attack Detection Modules** section and click the icon. In this example, the module is **SQL Injection Detection Module**. anagement ii. In the **SQL Injection Detection Module** panel, configure the parameters and click **OK**. The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Enabled | The status of the detection module. |
| Blocking Threshold | The range of attacks that you want WAF to block. Valid values: Not Forbid, Only Forbid High Risk, Forbid Medium or High Risk, and Forbid All. |
| Record Threshold | The range of attacks that you want WAF to record. Valid values: Not Record, Only Record High Risk, Record Medium or High Risk, and Record All. |
| Detect Non-Injected SQL | The detection status of non-injection SQL attacks. |

6. Manage a protection policy.
To delete a protection policy, perform the following steps: Select the protection policy. In the upper-right corner, choose **More > Delete Selected Protection Policies**. In the message that appears, click **OK**.

###### 9.2.1.1.3 Create a custom rule

You can create custom rules to meet different requirements for intrusion protection and filter out specific requests. This topic describes how to create a custom rule for Web Application Firewall (WAF).

**Create a custom rule**

1.
2. In the top navigation bar, choose **Security Management > Network Security > Web**
**Application Firewall**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Protection Configuration > Customized Rules**.
4. In the upper-right corner, click **Add Rule**. In the Add Customized Rules panel, configure the
parameters and click **OK**. The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Type | The action that you want WAF to perform on requests that match the rule. Valid values: Block: blocks requests that match the rule. Allow: allows requests that match the rule. Monitor: records and allows requests that match the rule. Detection module control |

anagement

| Comment | The description of the rule. We recommend that you enter the protection purpose of the rule. |
|---|---|
| Risk Level | The risk level. Valid values: No Threat, Low Risk, Medium Risk, and High Risk. Note This parameter is required only if you set the Type parameter to Block, Allow, or Monitor. |
| Matching Pattern | The match conditions of the rule. Click Add Pattern to specify more than one condition. A request matches the rule only if the request matches all match conditions. For example, if you want to block requests from a specific path of an HTTPS proxy that is added to WAF, you can set the Type parameter to Block and add the path to the match conditions. |
| Apply to Websites | The websites for which you want the rule to take effect. You cannot enter a website name that contains the wildcard character (*). |
| Log Recording Option | Specifies whether to record a log when the rule is triggered. The default value is Enable Log Recording. After Log Recording Option is set to Enable Log Recording, all interception events are recorded in the intrusion detection logs. |
| Attack Type | The type of attack that you want to defend against. |
| Blocking Status Code | The status code that you want the website to return when a request is blocked. |
| Expiration Time | The expiration time of the rule. |

5. (Optional) You can create custom rules offline and click **Import Rules** to import the rules at
the same time.

**Configuration example**

If you want to block all requests from an HTTPS proxy that is added to WAF except requests from a specific path, you can set the protection action of the protection policy for the HTTPS proxy to Block and create a custom rule. This section provides a sample configuration.
**Type**: Set the value to **Allow**.
**Matching Pattern**: Set the match field to **URI**, the logical operator to **contain**, and the
match content to the path.
**Apply to Websites**: Select the domain name of the HTTPS proxy.
anagement

**Manage custom rules**

You can view and manage custom rules in the custom rule list. View custom rules In the custom rule list, view the custom rules that you created. Multiple custom rules are evaluated by using the logical **OR** operator. If two custom rules use the same match conditions but trigger different actions, such as blocking traffic or allowing traffic, WAF runs the first rule. Modify a custom rule Find the rule that you want to modify and click the icon in the **Actions** column. Filter custom rules In the upper-right corner of the Customized Rules page, click **Filter**. In the Filter Item panel, specify filter conditions to filter custom rules by ID, comment, most recent modification time, creation time, or expiration time. Enable, disable, or delete custom rules Select the rules that you want to manage and then choose **More > Enable Selected**
**Rules**, **Disable Selected Rules**, or **Delete Selected Rules** to enable, disable, or delete
the rules.

###### 9.2.1.1.4 Configure an HTTP flood protection rule

An HTTP flood attack is a type of DDoS attack that targets the application layer. Attackers use proxy servers or zombies to overwhelm targeted web servers by sending a large number of HTTP requests. This topic describes how to configure an HTTP flood protection rule.

**Create an HTTP flood protection rule**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console.
2. In the upper-right corner of the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console, choose
**Security** > **Application Security > Web Application Firewall**. On the **Web**
**Application Firewall** page, select a **region** and click **Access with Authorized Role**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Protection Configuration** > **HTTP Flood**
**Detection**.
anagement
4. Click **Add Rule**. In the **Add HTTP Flood Detection Rules** panel, configure the parameters
and click **Confirm**. The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Rule Mode | The action that you want WAF to perform on requests that trigger the HTTP flood protection rule. Valid values: Blocking Mode and Observe. Blocking Mode: limits the requests. Observe: records but does not limit the requests. |
| Rule Types | The type of the HTTP flood protection rule. Valid values: Restrict Users by Policy and Restrict Known Users. Restrict Users by Policy: limits requests that meet all the match conditions in the HTTP flood protection rule. You can specify the following match conditions: Restriction Trigger Threshold, Restricted URL Address, Restriction Mode, Restriction Time, and Statistical Range of Visits. The Statistical Range of Visits parameter is in the Advanced section. Restrict Known Users: limits requests that are initiated from specific IP addresses or in specific sessions based on the HTTP flood protection rule. To restrict known users, you must configure the IP address or session list and the limit mode. After you configure the list, the HTTP flood protection rule limits requests based on the list. |
| Rule Name | The name of the HTTP flood protection rule. |
| Target Type | The type of source for limited requests. Valid values:I P and SESSION. Note If you set Target Type to SESSION, you can apply the HTTP protection rule only to a website whose User Identification is set to WAF User System. For more information, see Add an Internet website to WAF for protection. |
| Restriction Trigger Threshold | If you set Rule Types to Restrict Users by Policy, you must configure the triggering conditions for the HTTP flood protection rule. |

anagement

| Restricted URL Address | If you set Rule Types to Restrict Users by Policy, you must specify the URL addresses that are protected based on the HTTP flood protection rule. URL Prefix URL Record all IP addresses |
|---|---|
| Restricted IP List or Restricted SESSION List | If you set Rule Types to Restrict Known Users, you must enter the IP addresses or sessions from which you want to limit requests based on the value of Target Type. You can enter only one IP address or session in each line. |
| Restricted URL Address | If you set Rule Types to Restrict Known Users, you must specify the URL addresses that are protected based on the HTTP flood protection rule. URL Prefix URL Restrict user access to all addresses |
| Restriction Mode | The mode in which the HTTP flood protection rule limits requests. Valid values: Forbidden: The rule blocks specific sources from accessing the specified URL address. Frequency control: The rule limits the frequency at which specific sources access the specified URL address. |
| Restriction Time | The time at which the action specified in the HTTP flood protection rule takes effect. |
| Statistical Range of Visits | If you set Rule Type to Restrict Users by Policy, you can specify the range of data records to limit requests in the Advanced section. Statistics Full Access Data: If you select this option, the frequency of requests is limited when the requests are forwarded to WAF and meet the HTTP flood protection rule, regardless of which data records are accessed by requests. This decreases system performance. Statistics TOP Access Data: If you select this option, the frequency of requests is limited when the requests meet the preceding conditions and access the top 100 data records. This option helps reduce the decrease in system performance. You can select this option when the number of accessed data records is greater than 100. Take note that the top 100 data records are measured based on real-time monitoring. |

**Manage HTTP flood protection rules**

You can view and manage HTTP flood protection rules in the HTTP flood protection rule list. View HTTP flood protection rules anagement In the HTTP flood protection rule list, you can view the protection policies, binding situations, creation time, and most recent modification time. Modify HTTP flood protection rules Find the HTTP flood protection rule that you want to modify and click the icon in the
**Actions** column.
Filter HTTP flood protection rules In the upper-right corner of the page, click **Filter** to filter HTTP flood protection rules by ID, name, target type, and creation time. Enable, disable, or delete HTTP flood protection rules Select the HTTP flood protection rules that you want to manage and select **Enable**
**Selected Rules**, **Disable Selected Rules**, or **Delete Selected Rules** from the **More**
drop-down list.

##### 9.2.1.3 System management

###### 9.2.1.3.1 Configure global system settings

You can configure global system settings for Web Application Firewall (WAF) to enable the global protection engine, specify the upper limit of downloaded logs, and enable traffic forwarding for the HTTPS proxy. This topic describes how to configure global system settings. 1.
2. In the top navigation bar, choose **Security Management > Network Security > Web**
**Application Firewall**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **System Settings > Global System Settings**.
4. On the **Global System Settings** page, configure the parameters. The following table
describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description | Operation |
|---|---|---|

anagement

| Global WAF Protection Engine | The global protection engine determines the status of intrusion prevention configurations at the WAF platform management side and the service group management side. If you turn off Global WAF Protection Engine, WAF allows all traffic and does not perform intrusion detection or traffic processing. | Click the icon to the right of this parameter. In the panel that appears, turn on or turn off the switch and click OK. |
|---|---|---|
| HTTPS-proxy Traffic Forwarding | Specifies whether to enable HTTPS proxy traffic forwarding. |   |
| Ingress Traffic Forwarding | Specifies whether to enable ingress traffic forwarding. |   |
| Maximum Number of Journal Downloads | Specifies the maximum number of logs that can be downloaded. | Click the icon on the right side of this parameter and specify the maximum number of logs that can be downloaded. Then, click OK. |
